S_VWAPT_rnd_sbc_gpa.expr:
# Thesis: blend a late-day liquidity-reversal signal with three slow, unrelated quality/investment signals. The slow parts dilute the overlap with crowded reversal alphas while adding their own premia.
# Source: liquidity reversal (Campbell, Grossman & Wang, QJE 1993); R&D intensity (Chan, Lakonishok & Sougiannis, JF 2001); gross profitability (Novy-Marx, JFE 2013, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2013.01.003); stock-based pay as an intangible-investment proxy, like R&D (our own hypothesis, no single source)
g = ts_mean((close - vwap_last_hour)/vwap_last_hour, 5)  # 5-day avg close-vs-VWAP gap, in %
busy = cs_rank(number_of_trades_last_hour/ts_mean(number_of_trades_last_hour, 20)) > 1.3  # unusually many last-hour trades
r = cs_zscore(at_zero2nan(-cs_rank(g) * busy))  # fade the gap on busy closes
k1 = cs_zscore(cs_rank(ts_fill(research_and_development_expense)/mktcap))  # R&D intensity: long high R&D per dollar of market value
k2 = cs_zscore(cs_rank(ts_fill(stock_based_compensation)/mktcap))  # stock-based pay per dollar of market value
k3 = cs_zscore(cs_rank(ts_fill(gross_profit)/ts_fill(total_assets)))  # gross profitability: gross profit per dollar of assets
alpha = at_zero2nan(at_nan2zero(r) + at_nan2zero(k1) + at_nan2zero(k2) + at_nan2zero(k3))  # equal-weight blend; NaN parts count as 0

Q_52WH.expr:
# Thesis: investors anchor on the 52-week high, so stocks trading near it under-react to good news and keep drifting up; stocks far below it keep lagging.
# Source: George & Hwang, "The 52-Week High and Momentum Investing" (Journal of Finance 2004).
near = close/ts_max(close, 250)  # price as a fraction of its 52-week high (1 = at the high)
alpha = cs_indneut(cs_rank(near), subindustry)  # long near-high, short far-below, within each sub-industry

Q_FROG.expr:
# Thesis: momentum built from many small steady moves ("frog in the pan") is under-noticed and persists; momentum from a few big jumps gets priced fast.
# Source: Da, Gurun & Warachka, "Frog in the Pan: Continuous Information and Momentum" (Review of Financial Studies 2014).
pret = close/ts_delay(close, 250) - 1  # past 12-month return
sgn = (pret > 0)*2 - 1  # +1 winners, -1 losers
idisc = sgn*(ts_mean(ret1 < 0, 250) - ts_mean(ret1 > 0, 250))  # information discreteness: low = continuous (many small same-sign days)
alpha = cs_rank(pret) * (2 - cs_rank(idisc))  # momentum, amplified where information arrived continuously (nonlinear interaction)

Q_TUGOFWAR.expr:
# Thesis: different clienteles trade overnight (retail, at the open) and intraday (institutions); overnight strength persists while intraday strength reverses, so the gap between them predicts returns.
# Source: Lou, Polk & Skouras, "A Tug of War: Overnight versus Intraday Expected Returns" (Journal of Financial Economics 2019).
ovn = open/ts_delay(close, 1) - 1  # overnight return (close to next open)
intra = close/open - 1  # intraday return (open to close)
alpha = cs_rank(ts_mean(ovn, 20)) - cs_rank(ts_mean(intra, 20))  # long overnight winners, short intraday winners, 1-month averages

Q_HVRP.expr:
# Thesis: an unusual volume spike without a big price move raises a stock's visibility, bringing new buyers and higher returns over the next weeks.
# Source: Gervais, Kaniel & Mingelgrin, "The High-Volume Return Premium" (Journal of Finance 2001).
vshock = ts_mean(volume, 5)/ts_mean(volume, 60)  # last week's volume vs the past quarter
quiet = cs_rank(abs(ts_mean(ret1, 5))) < 1.5  # price barely moved, so the spike is attention, not news
alpha = at_zero2nan(cs_rank(vshock) * quiet)  # long volume shocks in quiet-price stocks

Q_VALxQUAL.expr:
# Thesis: cheap stocks are often cheap for a reason; cheap AND profitable stocks are the true bargains, so value and quality interact rather than add.
# Source: Piotroski, "Value Investing: The Use of Historical Financial Statement Information" (Journal of Accounting Research 2000); Asness, Frazzini & Pedersen, "Quality Minus Junk" (Review of Accounting Studies 2019).
v = cs_rank(ts_fill(earnings_yield))  # earnings yield rank (cheapness)
q = cs_rank(ts_fill(return_on_assets))  # return on assets rank (profitability)
alpha = cs_zscore(v * q)  # product: rewards stocks that are both cheap and profitable (nonlinear)

Q_ACCR_AG.expr:
# Thesis: earnings made of accruals rather than cash, and aggressive balance-sheet growth, are both over-extrapolated by investors and later disappoint.
# Source: Sloan, "Do Stock Prices Fully Reflect Information in Accruals and Cash Flows about Future Earnings?" (The Accounting Review 1996); Cooper, Gulen & Schill, "Asset Growth and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns" (Journal of Finance 2008).
ta = ts_fill(total_assets)  # total assets, filled between reports
acc = (ts_fill(net_income) - ts_fill(cash_from_operations))/ta  # accruals scaled by assets
ag = ta/ts_delay(ta, 250) - 1  # one-year asset growth
alpha = at_zero2nan(at_nan2zero(cs_zscore(-cs_rank(acc))) + at_nan2zero(cs_zscore(-cs_rank(ag))))  # short high accruals and fast asset growth

Q_BAB.expr:
# Thesis: leverage-constrained investors buy high-beta stocks to get market exposure, overpricing them; low-beta stocks earn more per unit of risk.
# Source: Frazzini & Pedersen, "Betting Against Beta" (Journal of Financial Economics 2014).
rho = ts_corr_binary(ret1, ret1_spx, 250)  # 1-year correlation with the S&P 500
beta = rho*ts_std(ret1, 250)/(ts_std(ret1_spx, 250) + 0.000001)  # market beta = correlation x volatility ratio
alpha = -cs_rank(beta)  # long low beta, short high beta

Q_MAX_RETAIL.expr:
# Thesis: lottery-like stocks (a huge one-day jump last month) are overbought by gambling retail investors; the effect should be strongest where trading is retail-sized.
# Source: Bali, Cakici & Whitelaw, "Maxing Out" (Journal of Financial Economics 2011); Kumar, "Who Gambles in the Stock Market?" (Journal of Finance 2009).
mx = ts_max(ret1, 20)  # biggest daily return in the past month
small = cs_rank(ts_mean(volume_last_hour/number_of_trades_last_hour, 20)) < 1.5  # small average trade size (retail-like)
alpha = at_zero2nan(-cs_rank(mx) * small)  # short lottery stocks where retail dominates (nonlinear gate)

Q_LEADLAG.expr:
# Thesis: news about a sub-industry is priced first in its big, well-followed firms; small firms catch up with a lag, so a small firm's peer-group return predicts its own.
# Source: Hou, "Industry Information Diffusion and the Lead-Lag Effect in Stock Returns" (Review of Financial Studies 2007).
r5 = ts_mean(ret1, 5)  # own 5-day average return
peer = r5 - cs_indneut(r5, subindustry)  # sub-industry average 5-day return
smallcap = cs_rank(at_signlog(mktcap)) < 1.5  # smaller half of the universe, where the lag is largest
alpha = at_zero2nan(cs_rank(peer) * smallcap)  # long small firms whose sub-industry just rose, short those whose sub-industry fell (own return not used, so this is not a reversal)

Q_EPSMOM.expr:
# Thesis: investors under-react to earnings changes, so stocks whose trailing EPS just rose (relative to price) keep drifting up for months (post-earnings drift without the earnings-date variable).
# Source: Bernard & Thomas, "Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift" (Journal of Accounting Research 1989); Chan, Jegadeesh & Lakonishok, "Momentum Strategies" (Journal of Finance 1996).
eps = ts_fill(trailing_12_month_diluted_eps)  # trailing 12-month diluted EPS, filled between reports
surp = (eps - ts_delay(eps, 60))/close  # EPS change over a quarter, per dollar of price
alpha = cs_rank(at_zero2nan(surp))  # long recent EPS improvers; no change (no new report) = no position

r = cs_zscore(at_zero2nan(-cs_rank(ts_mean(return_last_hour, 5)) * late))  # fade last-hour returns where the close was volatile
k1 = cs_zscore(cs_rank(ts_fill(stock_based_compensation)/mktcap))  # stock-based pay per dollar of market value
k2 = cs_zscore(-cs_rank(shsout/ts_delay(shsout, 250) - 1))  # net issuance: short dilution, long buybacks

U_VWAPT_szvo.expr:
# Thesis: a close far from the last-hour VWAP on a busy close marks temporary liquidity pressure, which reverses.
# Source: high-volume liquidity reversal (Campbell, Grossman & Wang, QJE 1993); closing-pressure reversal (Bogousslavsky & Muravyev 2023).
# Upgrade: positions are neutralized to size and volatility, the shared tilts most crowded alphas carry, so what remains is the stock-specific part of the signal (Isichenko 2021; WorldQuant BRAIN "regress out correlated components").
g = ts_mean((close - vwap_last_hour)/vwap_last_hour, 5)  # 5-day avg close-vs-VWAP gap, in %
busy = cs_rank(number_of_trades_last_hour/ts_mean(number_of_trades_last_hour, 20)) > 1.3  # unusually many last-hour trades
sz = cs_rank(at_signlog(mktcap))  # size rank (log market cap)
vo = cs_rank(ts_std(ret1, 20))  # 1-month volatility rank
alpha = cs_factorneut(at_zero2nan(-cs_rank(g) * busy), [sz, vo])  # fade the gap on busy closes, then size- and volatility-neutral

U_PRICE2_szvo.expr:
# Thesis: equal-weight mix of two late-day reversal signals (busy-close VWAP gap, and the heavy-volume late-day composite); late flow pushes prices that partly reverse.
# Source: Bogousslavsky & Muravyev, "Who Trades at the Close?" (2023); Campbell, Grossman & Wang (QJE 1993).
# Upgrade: positions are neutralized to size and volatility, the shared tilts most crowded alphas carry, so what remains is the stock-specific part of the signal (Isichenko 2021; WorldQuant BRAIN "regress out correlated components").
g = ts_mean((close - vwap_last_hour)/vwap_last_hour, 5)  # 5-day avg close-vs-VWAP gap, in %
busy = cs_rank(number_of_trades_last_hour/ts_mean(number_of_trades_last_hour, 20)) > 1.3  # unusually many last-hour trades
p1 = cs_zscore(at_zero2nan(-cs_rank(g) * busy))  # fade the gap on busy closes
a = cs_rank(ts_mean(return_last_hour, 5))  # 5-day avg last-hour return
b = cs_rank(ts_mean((close_price_last_hour - low_price_last_hour)/(high_price_last_hour - low_price_last_hour + 0.0001*close), 5))  # where the close sits in the last-hour range
hot = cs_rank(volume/ts_mean(volume, 20)) > 1.3  # volume above its 20-day norm
p2 = cs_zscore(at_zero2nan(-(a + b + cs_rank(g)) * hot))  # fade the late-day composite on heavy volume
sz = cs_rank(at_signlog(mktcap))  # size rank (log market cap)
vo = cs_rank(ts_std(ret1, 20))  # 1-month volatility rank
alpha = cs_factorneut(at_zero2nan(at_nan2zero(p1) + at_nan2zero(p2)), [sz, vo])  # equal-weight sum, then size- and volatility-neutral

alpha = cs_factorneut(at_zero2nan(at_nan2zero(r) + at_nan2zero(k1) + at_nan2zero(k2) + at_nan2zero(k3)), [sz, vo])  # equal-weight blend; NaN parts count as 0, then size- and volatility-neutral

U_FMOM5.expr:
# Thesis: improving fundamentals (rising profitability and cash flow, falling leverage, better asset turnover and margins) are under-reacted to, so the CHANGE in a firm's financial health predicts returns even when its level does not.
# Source: Piotroski, "Value Investing: The Use of Historical Financial Statement Information to Separate Winners from Losers" (Journal of Accounting Research 2000); Soliman, "The Use of DuPont Analysis by Market Participants" (The Accounting Review 2008).
ta = ts_fill(total_assets)  # total assets, filled between reports
roa = ts_fill(return_on_assets)  # return on assets
d1 = cs_zscore(cs_rank(roa - ts_delay(roa, 250)))  # one-year change in ROA
cf = ts_fill(cash_from_operations)/ta  # operating cash flow per dollar of assets
d2 = cs_zscore(cs_rank(cf - ts_delay(cf, 250)))  # one-year change in cash-flow profitability
lev = ts_fill(total_debt)/ta  # leverage
d3 = cs_zscore(-cs_rank(lev - ts_delay(lev, 250)))  # falling leverage is good
tu = ts_fill(sales_to_total_assets_ratio)  # asset turnover
d4 = cs_zscore(cs_rank(tu - ts_delay(tu, 250)))  # rising asset turnover
gm = ts_fill(gross_profit)/ts_fill(net_sales)  # gross margin
d5 = cs_zscore(cs_rank(gm - ts_delay(gm, 250)))  # rising gross margin
alpha = at_zero2nan(at_nan2zero(d1) + at_nan2zero(d2) + at_nan2zero(d3) + at_nan2zero(d4) + at_nan2zero(d5))  # equal-weight fundamental-momentum score

U_ILLIQ_rig_szvo.expr:
# Thesis: blend a late-day liquidity-reversal signal with three slow, unrelated quality/investment signals. The slow parts dilute the overlap with crowded reversal alphas while adding their own premia.
# Source: liquidity reversal (Campbell, Grossman & Wang, QJE 1993); R&D intensity (Chan, Lakonishok & Sougiannis, JF 2001); gross profitability (Novy-Marx, JFE 2013, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2013.01.003); net share issuance (Pontiff & Woodgate, JF 2008), a public proxy for insider/management timing of buybacks and issues
# Upgrade: positions are neutralized to size and volatility, the shared tilts most crowded alphas carry, so what remains is the stock-specific part of the signal (Isichenko 2021; WorldQuant BRAIN "regress out correlated components").
g = ts_mean((close - vwap_last_hour)/vwap_last_hour, 5)  # 5-day avg close-vs-VWAP gap, in %
illiq = cs_rank(ts_mean(ret1*ret1/(volume*close), 20)) > 1.5  # more illiquid half (squared-return Amihud variant)
hot = cs_rank(volume/ts_mean(volume, 20)) > 1.3  # volume above its 20-day norm
r = cs_zscore(at_zero2nan(-cs_rank(g) * hot * illiq))  # fade the gap in illiquid stocks on heavy days
k1 = cs_zscore(cs_rank(ts_fill(research_and_development_expense)/mktcap))  # R&D intensity: long high R&D per dollar of market value
k2 = cs_zscore(-cs_rank(shsout/ts_delay(shsout, 250) - 1))  # net issuance: short firms growing share count (dilution), long buybacks
k3 = cs_zscore(cs_rank(ts_fill(gross_profit)/ts_fill(total_assets)))  # gross profitability: gross profit per dollar of assets
sz = cs_rank(at_signlog(mktcap))  # size rank (log market cap)
vo = cs_rank(ts_std(ret1, 20))  # 1-month volatility rank
alpha = cs_factorneut(at_zero2nan(at_nan2zero(r) + at_nan2zero(k1) + at_nan2zero(k2) + at_nan2zero(k3)), [sz, vo])  # equal-weight blend; NaN parts count as 0, then size- and volatility-neutral

U_VWAPT_FMOM_w2.expr:
# Thesis: late-day liquidity reversal blended (at 1:2) with a fundamental-momentum score; improving fundamentals (rising profitability and cash flow, falling leverage, better asset turnover and margins) are under-reacted to, so the CHANGE in a firm's financial health predicts returns even when its level does not.
# Source: Piotroski, "Value Investing: The Use of Historical Financial Statement Information to Separate Winners from Losers" (Journal of Accounting Research 2000); Soliman, "The Use of DuPont Analysis by Market Participants" (The Accounting Review 2008). Reversal: Campbell, Grossman & Wang (QJE 1993).
ta = ts_fill(total_assets)  # total assets, filled between reports
roa = ts_fill(return_on_assets)  # return on assets
d1 = cs_zscore(cs_rank(roa - ts_delay(roa, 250)))  # one-year change in ROA
cf = ts_fill(cash_from_operations)/ta  # operating cash flow per dollar of assets
d2 = cs_zscore(cs_rank(cf - ts_delay(cf, 250)))  # one-year change in cash-flow profitability
lev = ts_fill(total_debt)/ta  # leverage
d3 = cs_zscore(-cs_rank(lev - ts_delay(lev, 250)))  # falling leverage is good
tu = ts_fill(sales_to_total_assets_ratio)  # asset turnover
d4 = cs_zscore(cs_rank(tu - ts_delay(tu, 250)))  # rising asset turnover
gm = ts_fill(gross_profit)/ts_fill(net_sales)  # gross margin
d5 = cs_zscore(cs_rank(gm - ts_delay(gm, 250)))  # rising gross margin
g = ts_mean((close - vwap_last_hour)/vwap_last_hour, 5)  # 5-day avg close-vs-VWAP gap, in %
busy = cs_rank(number_of_trades_last_hour/ts_mean(number_of_trades_last_hour, 20)) > 1.3  # unusually many last-hour trades
r = cs_zscore(at_zero2nan(-cs_rank(g) * busy))  # late-day reversal: fade the gap on busy closes
alpha = at_zero2nan(at_nan2zero(r) + 2*(at_nan2zero(d1) + at_nan2zero(d2) + at_nan2zero(d3) + at_nan2zero(d4) + at_nan2zero(d5)))  # reversal + double-weight fundamental momentum

VP_VOV_D60.expr:
# Thesis: Stocks whose own volatility is unstable (high vol-of-vol) carry uncertainty about risk and underperform.
# Source: Baltussen, van Bekkum & van der Grient, "Unknown Unknowns" (JFQA 2018), https://ideas.repec.org/a/cup/jfinqa/v53y2018i04p1615-1651_00.html
vol = ts_std(ret1, 20)  # 20-day realized volatility
vov = ts_std(vol, 60) / ts_mean(vol, 60)  # vol-of-vol: dispersion of rolling vol scaled by its level
alpha = -cs_rank(vov)  # short high uncertainty-about-risk names, long stable-risk names

VP_VOV_INTRA.expr:
# Thesis: Vol-of-vol measured from intraday (first/last hour) volatility: unstable intraday risk predicts underperformance.
# Source: Baltussen, van Bekkum & van der Grient, "Unknown Unknowns" (JFQA 2018), https://ideas.repec.org/a/cup/jfinqa/v53y2018i04p1615-1651_00.html
iv = std_dev_return_first_hour + std_dev_return_last_hour  # intraday realized vol at both ends of the day
vov = ts_std(iv, 20) / ts_mean(iv, 20)  # day-to-day instability of intraday vol, scale-free
alpha = -cs_rank(ts_mean(vov, 5))  # short names with unstable intraday risk (5-day smoothed)

VP_COSK_60.expr:
# Thesis: Stocks that rally when the market makes big moves (positive coskewness, long-gamma-like) are overpriced; negative-coskew stocks earn a premium.
# Source: Harvey & Siddique, "Conditional Skewness in Asset Pricing Tests" (JF 2000), https://people.duke.edu/~charvey/Research/Published_Papers/P56_Conditional_skewness_in.pdf
m2 = ret1_spx * ret1_spx  # squared market return: a market variance shock
cosk = ts_corr_binary(ret1, m2, 60)  # coskewness proxy over 60 days
alpha = -cs_rank(cosk)  # long negative-coskew names, short positive-coskew (lottery-like) names

VP_COSK_RESID120.expr:
# Thesis: Coskewness of the idiosyncratic return (beta removed) isolates the systematic-skew premium from market beta.
# Source: Harvey & Siddique, "Conditional Skewness in Asset Pricing Tests" (JF 2000), https://people.duke.edu/~charvey/Research/Published_Papers/P56_Conditional_skewness_in.pdf
beta = ts_corr_binary(ret1, ret1_spx, 120) * ts_std(ret1, 120) / ts_std(ret1_spx, 120)  # 120-day market beta
res = ret1 - beta * ret1_spx  # idiosyncratic daily return
m2 = ret1_spx * ret1_spx  # squared market return
cosk = ts_corr_binary(res, m2, 120)  # residual coskewness over 120 days
alpha = -cs_rank(cosk)  # long negative residual coskewness

VP_RESREV_VIX.expr:
# Thesis: Liquidity-provision (reversal) returns rise with VIX, most in volatile names: fade 3-day idiosyncratic moves and tilt toward high-idio-vol names only when VIX is high versus its past year.
# Source: Nagel, "Evaporating Liquidity" (RFS 2012), https://econpapers.repec.org/RePEc:oup:rfinst:v:25:y:2012:i:7:p:2005-2039
beta = ts_corr_binary(ret1, ret1_spx, 60) * ts_std(ret1, 60) / ts_std(ret1_spx, 60)  # 60-day market beta
res = ret1 - beta * ret1_spx  # idiosyncratic daily return
vixr = ts_rank(close_vix, 250) - 1  # VIX regime in [0,1] versus the past year
volr = cs_winsor(cs_zscore(ts_std(res, 20)), 0.05, False)  # cross-sectional idiosyncratic-vol z-score, tails clipped
w = 1 + 0.5 * vixr * volr  # high VIX: overweight volatile names, underweight calm ones
alpha = -cs_zscore(ts_sum(res, 3)) * w  # residual 3-day reversal with a VIX-dependent cross-sectional tilt

MM1_TOXREV.expr:
# Thesis: market makers lose to informed (toxic) flow and earn from uninformed flow. A last-hour move that was smooth and one-directional (high |information ratio| within the hour) looks informed and tends to continue; a choppy move looks like noise or liquidity demand and reverts.
# Critic fix (Oct 6): see alphas/drafts/c2-newfam.critic.md
# Source: Easley, Lopez de Prado & O'Hara, "Flow Toxicity and Liquidity in a High-Frequency World" (Review of Financial Studies 2012), https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1695596
r = cs_zscore(ts_mean(return_last_hour, 5))  # 5-day average last-hour return, cross-sectional z-score
sz = cs_rank(ts_mean(abs(return_last_hour), 5))  # typical size of the last-hour move, rank 1..2
smooth = cs_rank(cs_rank(ts_mean(abs(information_ratio_last_hour), 5)) - sz)  # smoothness beyond what move size explains (|IR| alone mostly ranks move size), rank 1..2
alpha = -r * (1.5 - smooth)  # fade choppy moves (+0.5 weight), follow the smoothest ones (-0.5 weight)

MM2_SIZEREV.expr:
# Thesis: late-day moves made by small (retail-sized) trades revert; moves made by large (institutional) trades carry information and continue.
# Critic fix (Oct 6): see alphas/drafts/c2-newfam.critic.md
# Source: Barber, Odean & Zhu, "Do Retail Trades Move Markets?" (Review of Financial Studies 2009), https://ideas.repec.org/a/oup/rfinst/v22y2009i1p151-186.html; Hvidkjaer, "Small Trades and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns" (Review of Financial Studies 2008), https://econpapers.repec.org/article/ouprfinst/v_3a21_3ay_3a2008_3ai_3a3_3ap_3a1123-1151.htm
# Caveat: Barber, Odean & Zhu find small-trade imbalance continues for about a week before reversing over a year, so the sim decides whether the small-trade leg reverts at this 5-day horizon.
r = cs_zscore(ts_mean(return_last_hour, 5))  # 5-day average last-hour return, cross-sectional z-score
q = (volume_last_hour/number_of_trades_last_hour)/(volume_first_hour/number_of_trades_first_hour)  # today's close-hour vs open-hour average trade size (dimensionless)
size = cs_rank(ts_mean(q, 5)/ts_mean(q, 60))  # this week's trade size vs the stock's own 3-month norm (who made THIS move), rank 1..2
alpha = -r * (1.5 - size)  # fade moves made by small trades, follow moves made by large trades

MM3_CLOSEPRESS.expr:
# Thesis: when an unusually large share of the day's volume prints in the last hour (index rebalancing, fund flows), the close is pushed away from fair value and reverts.
# Source: Bogousslavsky & Muravyev, "Who Trades at the Close? Implications for Price Discovery and Liquidity" (Journal of Financial Markets 2023), https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/finmar/v66y2023ics1386418123000502.html
share = volume_last_hour/volume  # fraction of the day's volume traded in the last hour
spike = cs_rank(ts_mean(share, 5) / ts_mean(share, 60)) > 1.5  # last-hour share recently above its own 3-month norm (top half)
alpha = at_zero2nan(-cs_rank(ts_mean(return_last_hour, 5)) * spike)  # fade the 5-day last-hour return only on close-pressure stocks; others get no position

MO1_RESMOM.expr:
# Thesis: momentum in the stock-specific return, scaled by its volatility, has about half the risk of plain momentum and avoids momentum crashes.
# Source: Blitz, Huij & Martens, "Residual Momentum" (Journal of Empirical Finance 2011), https://www.econbiz.de/Record/residual-momentum-blitz-david/10009194616; Huij & Lansdorp, "Residual Momentum and Reversal Strategies Revisited" (2017), https://www.ssrn.com/abstract=2929306
# Note: the card's rolling 120-day beta feeding 250-day residual sums needs 120 + 250 = 370 days, over the Slow max of 300 (empty alpha). Fixed as in Blitz et al.: one beta over the 250-day formation window applied to the 12-1 month sums, with residual std = std(ret1)*sqrt(1 - corr^2) (exact for that beta). Same quantity, 250 days of history.
rho = ts_corr_binary(ret1, ret1_spx, 250)  # 1-year correlation with the S&P 500
beta = rho * ts_std(ret1, 250) / (ts_std(ret1_spx, 250) + 0.0001)  # 1-year market beta = corr * vol ratio
res = (ts_sum(ret1, 250) - ts_sum(ret1, 20)) - beta*(ts_sum(ret1_spx, 250) - ts_sum(ret1_spx, 20))  # 12-1 month residual return (market part removed)
sres = ts_std(ret1, 250) * at_signsqrt(1 - rho*rho)  # 1-year daily residual volatility
alpha = cs_rank(res / (sres + 0.0001))  # long high, short low volatility-scaled residual momentum

MO2_FROG2.expr:
# Thesis: momentum built from many small steady moves ("frog in the pan") is under-noticed and persists; momentum from a few big jumps gets priced fast.
# Critic fix (Oct 6): see alphas/drafts/c2-newfam.critic.md
# Source: Da, Gurun & Warachka, "Frog in the Pan: Continuous Information and Momentum" (Review of Financial Studies 2014), https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhu003
# Note: dtype-fixed rerun of Q_FROG, which crashed because a true/false flag went into ts_mean; flags are now cast to float32 with one*(...).
one = close/close  # float32 matrix of ones (NaN where no price), used to cast flags
pret = ts_delay(close, 20)/ts_delay(close, 250) - 1  # 12-1 month return (skips the latest month, as in the paper)
pos = ts_mean(one*(ret1 > 0), 250)  # share of up days over the year
neg = ts_mean(one*(ret1 < 0), 250)  # share of down days over the year
sgn = one*(pret > 0)*2 - 1  # +1 winners, -1 losers
alpha = (cs_rank(pret) - 1.5) * (2 - cs_rank(sgn*(neg - pos)))  # momentum, amplified where information arrived continuously (low information discreteness)

MO3_VOLMOM.expr:
# Thesis: past winners with LOW turnover keep winning (under-followed), while high-turnover winners are crowded and fade. Momentum is best where attention is low.
# Critic fix (Oct 6): see alphas/drafts/c2-newfam.critic.md
# Source: Lee & Swaminathan, "Price Momentum and Trading Volume" (Journal of Finance 2000), https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v55y2000i5p2017-2069.html
mom = close/ts_delay(close, 250) - close/ts_delay(close, 20)  # 12-1 month price momentum (12-month minus 1-month return)
turn = cs_rank(ts_mean(volume/shsout, 120))  # 6-month average daily turnover, rank 1..2
alpha = (cs_rank(mom) - 1.5) * (2.5 - turn)  # centred momentum rank (long winners, short losers), weighted up for low-turnover (low-attention) stocks

LIQ_TURNCV.expr:
# Thesis: stocks whose trading volume is erratic (high coefficient of variation) earn LOWER future returns even after controlling for the volume level; steady-volume names are priced cheaper and outperform.
# Critic fix (Oct 6): see alphas/drafts/c3-scrape.critic.md
# Source: Chordia, Subrahmanyam & Anshuman, "Trading Activity and Expected Stock Returns" (Journal of Financial Economics 2001), https://repository.iimb.ac.in/handle/2074/11853; qlib Alpha158 VSTD/WVMA features, https://github.com/microsoft/qlib/blob/main/qlib/contrib/data/loader.py
cv = ts_std(volume, 250)/ts_mean(volume, 250)  # 1-year CV of daily volume: always spans ~4 earnings spikes (dimensionless)
lvl = ts_mean(volume/shsout, 60)  # 3-month average share turnover: the volume-level control the paper uses
alpha = cs_factorneut(-cs_zscore(cv), [cs_zscore(lvl), cs_zscore(at_signlog(mktcap))])  # short erratic-trading names, long steady ones, beyond their turnover level

LIQ_ILLIQSHOCK.expr:
# Thesis: investors underreact to stock-level liquidity shocks. A fall in Amihud illiquidity versus the stock's own 1-year norm predicts higher returns (continuation) for months, and a rise predicts lower returns; inattention is the driver.
# Source: Bali, Peng, Shen & Tang, "Liquidity Shocks and Stock Market Reactions" (Review of Financial Studies 2014), https://ideas.repec.org/a/oup/rfinst/v27y2014i5p1434-1485..html
il = abs(ret1)/(volume*close + 1)  # Amihud price impact per dollar traded today (dollar volume is split-invariant)
shock = ts_mean(il, 20)/ts_mean(il, 250)  # this month's illiquidity vs the stock's own 1-year norm (ratio: dimensionless)
alpha = -cs_rank(shock)  # long names whose liquidity improved, short names whose liquidity dried up

MOMX_STMOM_HITURN.expr:
# Thesis: among last month's high-turnover stocks, last month's return CONTINUES (short-term momentum), while low-turnover stocks reverse; it is strongest in large, liquid names because traders underweight the information in heavily traded prices.
# Critic fix (Oct 6): see alphas/drafts/c3-scrape.critic.md
# Source: Medhat & Schmeling, "Short-term Momentum" (Review of Financial Studies 2022), https://repec.cepr.org/repec/cpr/ceprdp/DP15857.pdf
f = close/close  # float32 ones (NaN where no price), used to cast the flag
turn = ts_mean(volume/shsout, 20)  # last month's average daily share turnover (dimensionless)
hi = f*(cs_rank(turn) > 1.8)  # 1 for the top-20% turnover names, else 0
m = ts_delay(ret20, 5)  # last month's return skipping the final week (days t-25..t-5)
alpha = at_zero2nan((cs_rank(m) - 1.5)*hi)  # follow last month's return in the most-traded names only; the rest get no position

MOMX_SEASON_1Y.expr:
# Thesis: stocks tend to earn relatively high (or low) returns in the same calendar window every year, at annual lags, on top of momentum and reversal and independent of earnings announcements; with the 300-day lookback cap only the 1-year lag fits.
# Source: Heston & Sadka, "Seasonality in the Cross-Section of Stock Returns" (Journal of Financial Economics 2008), https://rhsmith.umd.edu/news/seasonality-stock-market-returns; implementation https://github.com/paperswithbacktest/awesome-systematic-trading/blob/main/static/strategies/12-month-cycle-in-cross-section-of-stocks-returns.py
# Note: lb 280 = 240-day lag + 20 days in case ret20 is built from in-window data + 20 margin.
s = ts_delay(ts_delay(ret20, 120), 120)  # 20-day return ending 240 trading days ago: the window around this date one year ago
alpha = cs_rank(s)  # long names that did well in this calendar window last year, short those that did badly

HR_HKS_PERIOD.expr:
# Thesis: returns in a given intraday interval CONTINUE at lags that are exact multiples of a trading day, for at least 40 days, because institutions trade at the same time each day; tomorrow's first and last hours sit inside our close-to-close hold, so past first-hour and last-hour returns (skipping the reversal week) predict them.
# Critic fix (Oct 6): see alphas/drafts/c3-scrape.critic.md
# Source: Heston, Korajczyk & Sadka, "Intraday Patterns in the Cross-Section of Stock Returns" (Journal of Finance 2010), https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v65y2010i4p1369-1407.html
a = ts_delay(ts_mean(return_first_hour, 40), 5)  # average first-hour return over days t-44..t-5 (skips the 1-week reversal zone)
b = ts_delay(ts_mean(return_last_hour, 40), 5)  # same for the last hour
m = ts_delay(ts_mean(ret1, 40), 5)  # plain return over the same t-44..t-5 window
alpha = cs_factorneut(cs_zscore(cs_rank(a)) + cs_zscore(cs_rank(b)), [cs_zscore(cs_rank(m))])  # bet that tomorrow's first and last hours repeat these same-hour patterns

FUND_ORGCAP.expr:
# Thesis: organization capital built through SG&A spending (key talent with firm-specific efficiency) is risky for shareholders, so firms with more of it than industry peers earn higher returns (about 4.7%/yr, unexplained by CAPM, FF3 or Carhart).
# Critic fix (Oct 6): see alphas/drafts/c3-scrape.critic.md
# Source: Eisfeldt & Papanikolaou, "Organization Capital and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns" (Journal of Finance 2013), https://www.tse-fr.eu/sites/default/files/medias/stories/SEMIN_09_10/FINANCE/eisfeldt.pdf
ato = ts_fill(sales_to_total_assets_ratio)  # asset turnover (sales / assets)
sga = ts_fill(sell_and_admin_exp_to_net_sales_ratio)*ato  # SG&A / assets: flow proxy for organization capital
alpha = cs_factorneut(cs_zscore(ts_mean(sga, 120)), [cs_zscore(ato)])  # 6-month SG&A intensity (stock proxy) beyond plain asset turnover; industry neutralisation makes it peer-relative

FUND_TAXMOM.expr:
# Thesis: the year-over-year change in tax expense carries news about core profitability beyond reported earnings; prices absorb it slowly, so it predicts returns over the next two quarters, separately from size, B/M, accruals and momentum.
# Critic fix (Oct 6): see alphas/drafts/c3-scrape.critic.md
# Source: Thomas & Zhang, "Tax Expense Momentum" (Journal of Accounting Research 2011), https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/joares/v49y2011i3p791-821.html
# Caveat: the paper scales the YoY tax change by assets; the growth-pct field is the closest available input, ranked so small or negative bases do not dominate.
g = cs_rank(ts_fill(income_tax_expense_year_growth_pct))  # YoY tax-expense growth, rank 1..2
p = cs_rank(ts_fill(pretax_income_year_growth_pct))  # YoY pre-tax book-income growth, rank 1..2
alpha = cs_factorneut(cs_zscore(g), [cs_zscore(p)])  # tax-expense news beyond book-income news

PV_CORD.expr:
# Thesis: when rallies come with volume surges and declines with volume drops (high correlation of daily return with volume change), the moves are attention- or hedging-driven and get unwound; Llorente et al. show that returns from risk-sharing trades reverse while speculative ones continue.
# Source: Microsoft qlib Alpha158 CORD feature (GitHub repository), https://github.com/microsoft/qlib/blob/main/qlib/contrib/data/loader.py; Llorente, Michaely, Saar & Wang, "Dynamic Volume-Return Relation of Individual Stocks" (Review of Financial Studies 2002), https://www.johnhcochrane.com/s/llorente_michaely_saar_wang_volume_rfs.pdf
# Caveat: the US sign is unverified; screen -cord and +cord in Fast.
dv = at_signlog(volume/ts_delay(volume, 1))  # log(1 + today's volume / yesterday's), exactly qlib's Log(x+1)
cord = ts_corr_binary(ret1, dv, 60)  # 3-month correlation of daily return with volume change
alpha = -cs_rank(cord)  # short names whose rallies come with volume surges, long the opposite

REG_VR_FLIP.expr:
# Thesis: The 5-day variance ratio sorts names into trending vs mean-reverting regimes: follow the week where VR is high, fade it where VR is low, skip random walks.
# Source: Lo & MacKinlay, "Stock Market Prices Do Not Follow Random Walks" (RFS 1988), https://www.nber.org/papers/w2168
vr = ts_std(ret5, 120) * ts_std(ret5, 120) / (5 * ts_std(ret1, 120) * ts_std(ret1, 120))  # Lo-MacKinlay 5-day variance ratio
z = cs_zscore(vr)  # variance ratio relative to the cross-section
tr = z > 0.5  # trending regime (positive autocorrelation)
mr = z < -0.5  # mean-reverting regime (negative autocorrelation)
s = tr * cs_zscore(ret5) - mr * cs_zscore(ret5)  # momentum in trenders, reversal in mean-reverters
alpha = at_zero2nan(s)  # no position in random-walk names

REG_VR_SMOOTH.expr:
# Thesis: Continuous variance-ratio gate at the 10-day horizon: the sign and size of the bet on the last two weeks scale with the stock's own autocorrelation regime.
# Source: Lo & MacKinlay, "Stock Market Prices Do Not Follow Random Walks" (RFS 1988), https://www.nber.org/papers/w2168
vr = ts_std(ret10, 250) * ts_std(ret10, 250) / (10 * ts_std(ret1, 250) * ts_std(ret1, 250))  # 10-day variance ratio over a year
g = cs_winsor(cs_zscore(vr), 0.05, False)  # regime score: >0 trending, <0 mean-reverting
alpha = cs_zscore(ret10) * g  # fade the move in low-VR names, follow it in high-VR names

R_RIGwk_k15.expr:
# Thesis: blend a late-day liquidity-reversal signal with three slow, unrelated quality/investment signals, size/vol neutral, traded once a week. The slow parts dilute the overlap with crowded reversal alphas while adding their own premia.
# Source: liquidity reversal (Campbell, Grossman & Wang, QJE 1993); R&D intensity (Chan, Lakonishok & Sougiannis, JF 2001); gross profitability (Novy-Marx, JFE 2013, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2013.01.003); net share issuance (Pontiff & Woodgate, JF 2008)
# Repair: slow part 1.5x (cuts turnover; playbook Route A rank 1). Parent R_RIG_weekly2 (#703370) IR .075, TVR .259, irtvr .147, corr .584 to #601796 (bar .169).
g = ts_mean((close - vwap_last_hour)/vwap_last_hour, 5)  # 5-day avg close-vs-VWAP gap
busy = cs_rank(number_of_trades_last_hour/ts_mean(number_of_trades_last_hour, 20)) > 1.3  # unusually many last-hour trades
r = cs_zscore(at_zero2nan(-cs_rank(g) * busy))  # fade the gap on busy closes
k1 = cs_zscore(cs_rank(ts_fill(research_and_development_expense)/mktcap))  # R&D intensity per dollar of market value
k2 = cs_zscore(-cs_rank(shsout/ts_delay(shsout, 250) - 1))  # net issuance: short dilution, long buybacks
k3 = cs_zscore(cs_rank(ts_fill(gross_profit)/ts_fill(total_assets)))  # gross profitability
sz = cs_rank(at_signlog(mktcap))  # size rank (log market cap)
vo = cs_rank(ts_std(ret1, 20))  # 1-month volatility rank
s = at_nan2zero(cs_factorneut(at_zero2nan(at_nan2zero(r) + 1.5*(at_nan2zero(k1) + at_nan2zero(k2) + at_nan2zero(k3))), [sz, vo]))  # blend, slow part x1.5, size/vol neutral

f1 = ts_delay(f0, 1)  # week started yesterday
f2 = ts_delay(f0, 2)  # week started 2 days ago
f3 = ts_delay(f0, 3)  # week started 3 days ago
alpha = at_zero2nan(f0*s + (1-f0)*(f1*ts_delay(s, 1) + (1-f1)*(f2*ts_delay(s, 2) + (1-f2)*(f3*ts_delay(s, 3) + (1-f3)*ts_delay(s, 4)))))  # hold the week-start book all week

busy = cs_rank(number_of_trades_last_hour/ts_mean(number_of_trades_last_hour, 20)) > 1.3  # unusually many last-hour trades
r = cs_zscore(at_zero2nan(-cs_rank(g) * busy))  # fade the gap on busy closes
k1 = cs_zscore(cs_rank(ts_fill(research_and_development_expense)/mktcap))  # R&D intensity per dollar of market value
k2 = cs_zscore(-cs_rank(shsout/ts_delay(shsout, 250) - 1))  # net issuance: short dilution, long buybacks
k3 = cs_zscore(cs_rank(ts_fill(gross_profit)/ts_fill(total_assets)))  # gross profitability
sz = cs_rank(at_signlog(mktcap))  # size rank (log market cap)
vo = cs_rank(ts_std(ret1, 20))  # 1-month volatility rank
s = at_nan2zero(cs_factorneut(at_zero2nan(at_nan2zero(r) + 1.5*(at_nan2zero(k1) + at_nan2zero(k2) + at_nan2zero(k3))), [sz, vo]))  # blend, slow part x1.5, size/vol neutral

REG_PKCC_REV.expr:
# Thesis: When Parkinson range variance exceeds close-to-close variance, intraday swings are noise that mean-reverts; fade the week only in those names.
# Source: Lo & MacKinlay, "Stock Market Prices Do Not Follow Random Walks" (RFS 1988), https://www.nber.org/papers/w2168
lr = at_signlog(high / low - 1)  # log(high/low), the daily range in log terms
pk = ts_mean(lr * lr, 20) / 2.7726  # Parkinson range variance (divided by 4 ln 2)
cc = ts_std(ret1, 20) * ts_std(ret1, 20)  # close-to-close variance
g = cs_zscore(pk / cc) > 0  # range vol high relative to close vol: noisy, mean-reverting names

REG_DNBETA_ASYM.expr:

# Source: Ang, Chen & Xing, "Downside Risk" (RFS 2006), https://www.nber.org/papers/w11824
dn = ret1_spx * (ret1_spx < 0)  # market return on down days only
up = ret1_spx * (ret1_spx > 0)  # market return on up days only
asym = ts_corr_binary(ret1, dn, 120) - ts_corr_binary(ret1, up, 120)  # downside minus upside comovement
alpha = cs_rank(ts_mean(asym, 5))  # long downside-exposed names (5-day smoothed)

REG_DNBETA_250.expr:
# Thesis: Downside beta over a year (covariance with the market on down days) carries a positive risk premium beyond plain beta.
# Source: Ang, Chen & Xing, "Downside Risk" (RFS 2006), https://www.nber.org/papers/w11824
dn = ret1_spx * (ret1_spx < 0)  # market return on down days only
dbeta = ts_corr_binary(ret1, dn, 250) * ts_std(ret1, 250) / ts_std(dn, 250)  # downside beta
beta = ts_corr_binary(ret1, ret1_spx, 250) * ts_std(ret1, 250) / ts_std(ret1_spx, 250)  # regular beta
alpha = cs_rank(dbeta - beta)  # long excess downside beta, hedging out plain beta

ID_TSIZE_SHIFT.expr:

shift = ts_mean(tsz, 5) / ts_mean(tsz, 120) - 1  # recent trade size versus its own half-year norm
alpha = cs_rank(shift)  # long names where trades got bigger, short where they shrank

ID_TSIZE_FLOW.expr:
# Thesis: Small-trade buying (positive first-hour returns on days with unusually small trades) marks retail-favored stocks that underperform for weeks.
# Source: Hvidkjaer, "Small Trades and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns" (RFS 2008), https://econpapers.repec.org/article/ouprfinst/v_3a21_3ay_3a2008_3ai_3a3_3ap_3a1123-1151.htm

ANOM_MAX20.expr:

A101_002.expr:

# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
dv = delta(at_signlog(volume), 2)  # 2-day change in log volume
oc = (close - open)/open  # open-to-close return

A101_003.expr:
# Thesis: A rising open price on rising volume over two weeks is crowded buying that fades. (Alpha #3, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991

A101_004.expr:

# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991

A101_006.expr:
# Thesis: Price-volume co-movement signals liquidity-driven moves that reverse. (Alpha #6, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991

A101_014.expr:
# Thesis: Accelerating returns combined with price-volume correlation tend to reverse. (Alpha #14, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
acc = delta(ret1, 3)  # 3-day change in daily return
alpha = -cs_rank(acc)*ts_corr_binary(open, volume, 10)  # short acceleration, scaled by open-volume corr

A101_015.expr:
# Thesis: Persistent high-price/volume co-movement marks crowded moves that fade. (Alpha #15, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
c = ts_corr_binary(cs_rank(high), cs_rank(volume), 3)  # 3-day corr of high-price rank and volume rank
alpha = -ts_sum(cs_rank(c), 3)  # short names where that corr stays high

A101_018.expr:
# Thesis: Large, volatile intraday bodies that track the open reverse. (Alpha #18, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
body = (close - open)/close  # open-to-close move as a fraction of price
vol = ts_std(abs(close - open)/close, 5)  # 5-day volatility of the intraday move
alpha = -cs_rank(vol + body + ts_corr_binary(close, open, 10))  # fade big, volatile, open-anchored moves

A101_020.expr:
# Thesis: Opening above yesterday's high, close and low is an overreaction that fades. (Alpha #20, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
g_hi = open/ts_delay(high, 1) - 1  # gap versus yesterday's high
g_cl = open/ts_delay(close, 1) - 1  # gap versus yesterday's close
g_lo = open/ts_delay(low, 1) - 1  # gap versus yesterday's low
alpha = -cs_rank(g_hi)*cs_rank(g_cl)*cs_rank(g_lo)  # short the stocks that gap up the most

A101_022.expr:
# Thesis: Rising high-price/volume correlation in volatile names precedes reversal. (Alpha #22, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
dc = delta(ts_corr_binary(high, volume, 5), 5)  # 5-day change in the 5-day high-volume corr
alpha = -dc*cs_rank(ts_std(close, 20)/close)  # weight by 20-day price volatility

A101_026.expr:
# Thesis: When volume and high-price both sit at local peaks together, the move is exhausted. (Alpha #26, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
c = ts_corr_binary(ts_rank(volume, 5), ts_rank(high, 5), 5)  # corr of 5-day volume and high ranks
alpha = -ts_max(c, 3)  # short names with the highest recent co-peaking

A101_033.expr:
# Thesis: Close above open (intraday gain) reverts the next day. (Alpha #33, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
alpha = cs_rank(open/close - 1)  # long stocks that fell from open to close

A101_034.expr:
# Thesis: Calm stocks that fell today rebound; short-term vol spikes and gains fade. (Alpha #34, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
vr = ts_std(ret1, 3)/ts_std(ret1, 5)  # short- over medium-horizon volatility
alpha = cs_rank((1 - cs_rank(vr)) + (1 - cs_rank(ret1)))  # low vol ratio and low return rank are long

A101_035.expr:
# Thesis: High-volume days with a weak range position and weak returns lead to rebounds. (Alpha #35, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
v = ts_rank(volume, 40)  # volume versus its last 40 days
r = 1 - ts_rank((close + high - low)/close, 20)  # low intraday range position versus history
alpha = v*r*(1 - ts_rank(ret1, 40))  # heavy volume, weak range position, weak return

A101_038.expr:
# Thesis: Stocks at a local price high that also rose intraday fade. (Alpha #38, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
alpha = -cs_rank(ts_rank(close, 10))*cs_rank(close/open)  # short high 10-day rank times intraday gain

A101_040.expr:
# Thesis: Volatile highs that move with volume mark crowded, reversing moves. (Alpha #40, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
hv = ts_std(high, 10)/close  # 10-day volatility of the high, as a fraction of price
alpha = -cs_rank(hv)*ts_corr_binary(high, volume, 10)  # short volatile, volume-driven highs

A101_041.expr:
# Thesis: A close-hour VWAP above the geometric mid of the day's range signals buying that fades. (Alpha #41, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
mid = (high*low)**0.5/close  # geometric mid of the day's range, relative to the close
alpha = mid - vwap_last_hour/close  # long when the last-hour VWAP sits below the mid

A101_043.expr:
# Thesis: Price drops on unusually high volume rebound. (Alpha #43, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
rv = ts_rank(volume/ts_mean(volume, 20), 20)  # relative volume versus its recent history
alpha = rv*ts_rank(-delta(close, 5)/close, 10)  # long recent losers that traded heavily

A101_044.expr:
# Thesis: High prices that coincide with high volume rank are exhausted. (Alpha #44, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
alpha = -ts_corr_binary(high, cs_rank(volume), 5)  # negative 5-day corr of high and volume rank

A101_050.expr:
# Thesis: Persistent co-movement of volume and VWAP ranks marks crowded trades. (Alpha #50, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
c = ts_corr_binary(cs_rank(volume), cs_rank(vwap_last_hour), 5)  # 5-day corr of volume rank and VWAP rank
alpha = -ts_max(cs_rank(c), 5)  # short the most persistent co-movers

A101_053.expr:
# Thesis: A change in where the close sits within the day's range reverts. (Alpha #53, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
pos = ((close - low) - (high - close))/(close - low + 0.001*close)  # close location within the day's range
alpha = -delta(pos, 10)  # fade the 10-day change in close location

A101_054.expr:
# Thesis: A close near the low on a gap-down open rebounds (delay-0 contrarian). (Alpha #54, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
loc = (low - close)/(low - high - 0.001*close)  # how far the close sits above the low, 0..1
alpha = -loc*(open/close)**5  # long closes near the low, scaled by the open-to-close drop

A101_055.expr:
# Thesis: Stochastic-oscillator level moving with volume marks crowded moves. (Alpha #55, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
stoch = (close - ts_min(low, 10))/(ts_max(high, 10) - ts_min(low, 10) + 0.001*close)  # 10-day stochastic
alpha = -ts_corr_binary(cs_rank(stoch), cs_rank(volume), 5)  # short where stochastic and volume co-move

A101_009b.expr:
# Note: b-version = dtype-fixed rerun; the runner copy under the old tag is the crashing code (skipped).
# Thesis: Follow a move only when the last week was one-directional; otherwise fade it. (Alpha #9, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
up = (close/close)*(ts_min(ret1, 5) > 0)  # 1.0 if every day of the last 5 was up
dn = (close/close)*(ts_min(-ret1, 5) > 0)  # 1.0 if every day of the last 5 was down
trend = up + dn  # 1.0 if the week was one-directional
alpha = trend*ret1 - (1 - trend)*ret1  # momentum in clean trends, reversal otherwise

A101_012b.expr:
# Note: b-version = dtype-fixed rerun; the runner copy under the old tag is the crashing code (skipped).
# Thesis: A price move made on rising volume reverses next day (liquidity shock). (Alpha #12, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991
dv = delta(volume, 1)/ts_mean(volume, 20)  # change in volume, scaled by average volume
sg = (close/close)*(dv > 0) - (close/close)*(dv < 0)  # sign of the volume change as float32 (+1/-1)
alpha = -sg*ret1  # fade today's return in the direction of the volume change

A101_030b.expr:
# Note: b-version = dtype-fixed rerun; the runner copy under the old tag is the crashing code (skipped).
# Thesis: Three straight up-closes on fading volume is a weak rally to sell. (Alpha #30, adapted)
# Source: Kakushadze, "101 Formulaic Alphas" (2016), https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00991

alpha = (1 - cs_rank(s1 + s2))*ts_sum(volume, 5)/ts_sum(volume, 20)  # fewer up days and higher recent volume is better

ad = cs_zscore(cs_rank(ts_fill(accumulated_depreciation)/ta))  # accumulated depreciation (older asset base) per dollar of assets, ranked and z-scored
